subject: mathematics
question_text: If A is the matrix with rows (1, −2, 3), (2, 3, −1) and (−3, 1, 2), and B is the matrix with rows (1, 0, 2), (0, 1, 2) and (1, 2, 0), then check whether A and B commute under matrix multiplication.

mark_split.label: Compare the two products entry by entry

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.45, chapter 5 MATRICES, Short Answer question 17. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1+1+1 shape treats the two products as equal work and keeps a whole mark for the comparison and a whole mark for the verdict, because this question is decided by the comparison, not by the multiplication — a student who computes both products correctly and then writes "so they commute" has answered it wrongly. STEM WORDING: the source index words this as "verify that A and B commute". They do not. Computed independently before authoring: AB has rows (4, 4, −2), (1, 1, 10) and (−1, 5, −4); BA has rows (−5, 0, 7), (−4, 5, 3) and (5, 4, 1). All nine entries differ, so AB ≠ BA. The source's own printed conclusion is also AB ≠ BA, so the book's instruction contradicts the book's answer. The question is authored here as a CHECK, which is the only reading under which the stem and the mathematics agree; nothing was silently repaired and the disagreement is recorded here and reported. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B prints eight short answers of which the student writes any six, each worth 4 marks, under the 2026-27 pattern; Matrices supplies one of them. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would answer this — say what has to be worked out, what you compare, and what the answer turns out to be.

steps.label: Find AB
steps.margin_note: First mark. A and B commute only if AB = BA, so both products are needed. Multiply row by column: row 1 of A against column 1 of B is 1(1) + (−2)(0) + 3(1) = 4.
steps.memory_tip: Commuting means AB = BA, so one product proves nothing. Work out both.
lines: A and B commute only if AB = BA, so both
products have to be worked out.

recall.must_convey: That commuting means AB = BA, so both products are needed, and that AB is worked out first by row-into-column multiplication.
accept: commuting means AB equals BA so first work out AB by row into column
find the product A into B multiplying rows of A by columns of B
both products are needed so start with AB
commute ante AB equals BA, so modata AB compute cheyyali
multiply A by B row into column to get the first product

steps.why: The whole question is a comparison, so the answer is decided by two matrices, not one. Computing AB alone cannot settle anything either way.
common_mistakes: Multiplying entry by entry instead of row by column.
Working out only AB and assuming BA must match.

steps.label: Find BA
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Now B is on the left, so its rows meet A's columns. Row 1 of B against column 1 of A is 1(1) + 0(2) + 2(−3) = −5.
steps.memory_tip: In BA the rows of B meet the columns of A — the order of the two matrices decides everything.

recall.must_convey: That BA is worked out with B on the left, so the rows of B are multiplied by the columns of A.
accept: now find BA with B on the left so rows of B meet columns of A
multiply B into A the other way round
work out the second product BA by row into column
ippati B ni A tho multiply cheyyali, B rows and A columns
compute the product in the reverse order

steps.why: Swapping the order changes which rows meet which columns, so BA is a genuinely different calculation and not a rearrangement of the first answer.
common_mistakes: Copying AB and rearranging its entries instead of multiplying again.
Using the rows of A against the columns of B a second time.

steps.label: Compare the two
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Two matrices are equal only when EVERY matching pair of entries is equal. One unequal pair settles it, and here the very first pair, 4 against −5, already does.
steps.memory_tip: Two matrices are equal only if every matching pair of entries is equal, so one difference settles it.
lines: Compare the two matrices entry by entry.
In fact all nine matching entries differ.

recall.must_convey: That the two products are compared position by position and at least one matching pair is found to be different, for example 4 against −5 in the top-left.
accept: compare the matrices entry by entry and the top left is four in AB but minus five in BA
the matching entries are not the same so the matrices are different
even one unequal pair is enough and here every entry differs
entry by entry compare cheste anni different ga unnayi
position by position the two products do not agree

steps.why: Matrix equality is defined entry by entry, so a comparison has to name at least one pair that disagrees. "They look different" is not an argument an examiner can mark.
common_mistakes: Saying the matrices are different without naming a single differing entry.
Comparing an entry of AB with the wrong position of BA.

steps.label: State the conclusion
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The honest answer here is NO. Write it plainly: AB ≠ BA, so these two matrices do not commute. Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general, and this pair is an example.
steps.memory_tip: The honest answer is no. Write AB ≠ BA plainly rather than forcing the two products to agree.
lines: AB and BA are different matrices, so A and B
do not commute. Matrix multiplication is not
commutative in general, and this pair shows it.

lines.text: ∴ AB ≠ BA — A and B do not commute

recall.must_convey: That the verdict is stated: AB is not equal to BA, so A and B do not commute, and that matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.
accept: since AB is not equal to BA the two matrices do not commute
the answer is no they do not commute because the products differ
matrix multiplication is not commutative in general and this pair proves it
AB and BA same kaadu kabatti avi commute avvavu
state that A and B fail to commute

steps.why: A check question can end in no. Changing an entry to force AB = BA, or writing "hence they commute" after finding different matrices, throws away the mark the comparison just earned.
common_mistakes: Writing "hence they commute" out of habit after finding different products.
Recomputing until the two products agree instead of reporting the difference.
